title: Reading versus faking, and the Suburban Gardens story
summary: A story of failing a written dance number at Suburban Gardens, and why musicians should read.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: There were many names. But as you said before, Dick, I think that's a good thing to think about. While we're talking about these fellows, I don't know if you would say that they were all real jazz piano players. That is, in a real jazz sense. They may have been able to play with dance bands and play, but I think that they were more or less, most of some of these names that we mentioned, they were legitimate musicians. They played more or less by music, strictly. I don't know if they even played, if they were even able to fake. Because most of those old time musicians that read, they weren't too good at faking music. That gave a guy like me an advantage in those days. A lot of other guys that were coming up that could fake. I'll never forget, I was playing out at, I had a chance to go to work at Old Suburban Gardens in 1931 or 1932, I think it was. Johnny Detroit had the band out there. And there was a piano player playing out there then by the name of Wilbur Dinkle. There's another name. Now Wilbur Dinkle was a fine musician. Not too great a jazz musician, but he could read quite well. And I had the chance to take his place, he was leaving. And came out there and oh, there was some terrific act. There was a show going on and it was a terrific act. And they were playing this Mexican hat dance. And it was written in all sharps. A natural, B natural, F sharp. So Johnny Detroit put the music up, they gave it past the music out, you know. He counted off the beat. Well I got about two, I got about past three measures in that thing. And that was it, I was lost. So Johnny Detroit came around, he says, did you play in that, were you playing in that thing? I says, well Johnny, to tell you the truth. I says, no, I said, I played the first three measures. I said, after that, I said, I was lost. He says, well that's the trouble with you jazz musicians. He says, you see, when you get a chance to play something legitimate, he says, you can't do it. Well you see, there was a good example right there of the line between jazz musicians and legitimate musicians in those days. But Johnny was pretty nice about it. He says, well let's see what we got, let's see what we got coming next. He says, there was a girl singing. And she wanted to sing, I think it was Hussari Now. Well she didn't have the music for it. So she came to Johnny, she says, I want to do Hussari Now. Johnny says, have you got the music? Because Johnny was that way, you know, the acts had to have the music. So she says, no I don't have the music. He says, well how are we going to play it? So I told Johnny, I says, well I know it. I said, if you want to let me play it, I said, maybe some of the other guys know it. He says, well go ahead. So I ripped off an introduction for her and key, whatever key she wanted it in and started playing it. So the girl was so pleased about it that I could play it and a few of the other guys joined in and we faked it through. She says, well that, she says, that was real great. So Johnny Detroit says, well he said, you know something? He says, I got to give you credit kid. He says, you did a good job on that. He says, you know what you do with this other two? He says, take it home and woodshed it. He says, and maybe we can get through it. So I did. I took it home and woodshed it and came back and we played it. So you see, Dick, there was a good example. I'm glad I thought of that point. I mean, that was a good example of what the old musicians had to contend with, you see. In other words, we learned to play tunes, as I said, Harry Shields said, let's swing. We learned, we don't need any music on this. And we were content to go along and just play without music. But of course, there came a time when, if you had to play theater music or show music, that you did have to know something about reading music. And that's where a great line was drawn. But once again, I'm going to say that I kept studying. I said, well, I'm not going to be left behind. I said, I want to keep up with what's going on, you know. And I think that's a good thing for musicians to know how to read. I think that helps out quite a bit. I don't think that it should be that you don't know how to read music at all. That was a mistake that the old jazz musicians made.
